554.title: Peace on the messengers
554.hook: glory to your Lord, peace on the messengers, praise to Allah (37:180–182)
554.howItsDone: Many Muslims recite the last three verses of As-Saffat (37:180–182) to close a lesson, a gathering or a prayer, and send peace on the prophets whenever they are named.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Yunus, one of those who glorify, in the fish or long before it. Your line was glorifying got him out.

Some songs have a refrain you start waiting for. The verse changes, the story moves on, and then the chorus comes back, and you can almost sing it before it arrives. Surah As-Saffat has one. After several of its prophets' stories, the same short line returns: peace be on him. And at the very end, the refrain opens up to include every messenger at once, and the surah closes with three lines some Muslims use to close a gathering.

Listen back through As-Saffat. After Nuh's story: peace be on Nuh among the worlds. After Ibrahim's: peace be on Ibrahim. After Musa and Harun's: peace be on Musa and Harun. After Ilyas: peace be on Il-yasin. Each time, the Arabic begins salamun 'ala, peace upon. Four of the stories end that way, in peace, however hard they were. Then the surah's last three verses. First: glory to your Lord, the Lord of might, above what they describe. In the verse, that clears away every wrong picture of Allah. Then, Pickthall: "And peace be unto those sent (to warn). And praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds!" Now the refrain isn't for one prophet. It's for all of them, the named and the unnamed, everyone ever sent. And the last words go back to the opening of al-Fatiha: al-hamdu lillahi rabbi'l-'alamin, praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds. Three moves: glory, peace, praise. Glory says what Allah is above. Peace blesses those who carried His message. Praise says where everything belongs. Commentators, including Ibn Kathir, mention an early saying that whoever wants their reward measured out in full should end their gathering with these verses; its chain is discussed. Some Muslims recite them at the end of a lesson, a dinner, a meeting. Wishing peace on every messenger who ever lived is not a bad way to leave a room.
screen: `PRAISE TO THE LORD OF THE WORLDS.`

segments.voice: On one breath, think glory: the verse says God is beyond whatever is pictured. On the next, think peace, on every messenger, everyone who carried something true to people who didn't want it; on the next, praise, where everything belongs. If you pray, you can say the three verses in Arabic or in your own language.
Salamun, peace, the refrain that follows each prophet's story in As-Saffat, and widens at the end to bless every messenger. Today's word.
Your line: glory, peace, praise. The refrain, opened wide at the end. Day five hundred fifty-four, done.

555.title: Dawud and the two brothers
555.hook: two men climb the wall with a dispute over ewes, and Dawud realizes he was tested and repents (38:21–25)
555.howItsDone: Many Muslims perform a prostration of recitation (sajdat al-tilawa) at 38:24; schools differ on whether it is required or recommended, and Islamic legal teaching stresses hearing both parties before judging.

segments.voice: Yesterday: salamun, peace on every messenger at the close of As-Saffat. Your line was glory, peace, praise.

It's a private hour. Dawud is in his prayer chamber, and the commentators say no one was to come in. Then two men come over the wall. Not through the door. Over the wall. He's startled; the text says he was afraid. They say, quickly: don't be afraid. We're two parties in a dispute; one of us has wronged the other. Judge between us with truth, don't be unjust, and guide us to the right path. Then one of them tells his story, and Dawud answers before the text gives the other one a word.

Surah Sad, verse twenty-three. The first man says: this is my brother. He has ninety-nine ewes, and I have one ewe. And he said, give it to me, and he overpowered me in argument. Ninety-nine and one. And Dawud says, right away: he has wronged you by asking to add your ewe to his. Many partners wrong one another, except those who believe and do good, and how few they are. Then verse twenty-four, the turn. Dawud realized that We had tested him. He asked his Lord for forgiveness, fell down bowing, and turned back in repentance. What was the test? The Qur'an doesn't say, and commentators differ. Some later stories, known as Isra'iliyyat, tie it to an episode about another man's wife; many Muslim scholars, Ibn Kathir among them, set those stories aside, holding that prophets are protected from such a sin. A reading many find more convincing stays inside the scene: Dawud ruled after hearing only one side. The text never gives the second man a word. The story was built to make him judge fast, and he did. And the moment he saw it, he didn't defend himself. He went down on his face. Verse twenty-six gives the lesson to him directly: O Dawud, We have made you a successor on earth, so judge between people with truth, and don't follow desire. Many Muslims prostrate when they recite verse twenty-four; a hadith in Bukhari reports that Ibn 'Abbas saw the Prophet ﷺ prostrate there.
screen: `HE KNEW HE WAS TESTED, AND BOWED.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one recent judgment, about a coworker, a relative, someone online, where you heard one side and decided. Now give the other side a voice: what might they say, if they got to speak? You don't have to change your mind; just let the second man talk, and notice how it feels to hold the judgment a little more loosely.
Fitna, the trial that shows what's inside, the word behind Dawud's test after he ruled too quickly on the two brothers' dispute. Today's word.
Your line: judge, then look at yourself. Ninety-nine ewes, one ewe, and a second man who never spoke. See you tomorrow.

556.title: Ayyub's spring
556.hook: strike the ground with your foot: a cool spring to wash and drink (38:41–44)
556.howItsDone: Muslims hold up Ayyub as the model of sabr, patience in illness and loss; his cry in 21:83 is often recited by the sick, and his story is told to comfort those in long hardship.

segments.voice: Yesterday: fitna, Dawud's test, and a ruling made after hearing one side. Your line was judge, then look at yourself.

A hot afternoon, years of illness behind you, your body aching, and someone hands you a glass of cold water. You drink it slowly. Then you splash some on your face, the back of your neck, your wrists. For a moment, that's everything. In Surah Al-Anbiya, Ayyub cried: harm has touched me, and You are the most merciful. Surah Sad tells what happened next, and the answer to years of suffering arrives in the most ordinary form there is. Water. Under his own feet.

Surah Sad, verse forty-one. Remember Our servant Ayyub, when he called his Lord: Satan has touched me with weariness and torment. Then verse forty-two, the answer, as a command: urkud bi-rijlik, strike the ground with your foot. And there it is: a spring, cool water to wash in and to drink. He has to do something. Not much: one stamp of a weak foot. But the healing comes through that small act, and through water, the plainest gift of all. Verse forty-three: and We gave him back his family, and as many again with them, a mercy from Us and a reminder for those with understanding. Then a stranger detail. Verse forty-four: take a bundle of grass in your hand and strike with it, and don't break your oath. Commentators explain that during his illness Ayyub had sworn to strike someone, many say his wife, a set number of times. Allah gave him a gentle way to keep his word without harming her: one tap with a bundle of stalks. Mercy for him, and mercy for her. Then the verdict: We found him patient. How excellent a servant! He was always turning back. A hadith in Bukhari adds one more picture. After his healing, while Ayyub was bathing, a shower of golden locusts fell, and he began gathering them. His Lord called: didn't I make you rich enough? And Ayyub answered: yes, but I can never do without Your blessing.
screen: `A COOL SPRING TO WASH AND DRINK.`
`A BUNDLE OF GRASS, AN OATH KEPT.`

segments.voice: If you can, go to a sink, let the water run cold, and wash your face slowly, once, twice, three times, feeling it on your forehead, your eyes, your cheeks. If you can't get up, picture it in detail. Then sit, damp-faced, with Ayyub's spring: the answer to years of waiting, in the plainest gift there is.
Ayyub's spring. After long illness, Ayyub is told to strike the ground with his foot, and a cool spring rises for washing and drinking. Today's word.
Your line: patient; a spring came. Patient in the long hardship, and grateful for every small gift after it. Day five hundred fifty-six.

557.title: Iblis asks for time
557.hook: Iblis refuses again and asks for respite to mislead, except the sincere (38:71–83)
557.howItsDone: Muslims speak of ikhlas, sincerity, as doing every act for Allah alone, and many renew their intention (niyya) before prayer, charity and other good deeds.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ayyub's spring, cool water after years of illness. Your line was patient; a spring came.

Adam made from clay, the angels told to bow, and one who refused. Iblis, saying I'm better than him: You made me from fire and him from clay. This path met the scene back on day twenty-four, and the lesson was pride. Surah Sad tells it again, and lets it run a few lines further, past the refusal, into a negotiation. Iblis, expelled, doesn't beg to come back. He asks for something else. Time. And in his own boast, he admits there's someone he can't touch.

Verses seventy-one to seventy-six give the refusal: I am better than him. Then seventy-seven and seventy-eight: go out from here, you are rejected, and My curse is on you until the Day of Judgment. Verse seventy-nine. Iblis says: my Lord, then give me respite until the day they are raised. Notice two things. He still says my Lord; he doesn't deny Allah exists, he refuses Him. And he doesn't ask for forgiveness. He asks for time, to use against the people he refused to bow to. Allah answers: you are of those given respite, until the day of the known time. Then the boast, verses eighty-two and eighty-three. He swears by Allah's own might that he'll mislead every one of them, and then he adds the exception himself. Pickthall: "Save Thy single-minded slaves among them." The Arabic is al-mukhlasin, those made sincere, purified. The word is recited two ways in the established readings of the Qur'an: mukhlasin, those Allah has made sincere, and mukhlisin, those who make their worship sincere. Some scholars hold both meanings at once: sincerity is something a person works at, and something given. Either way, the enemy names his own limit. He can whisper to anyone. He can't take someone whose devotion is single-minded, done for Allah alone, not for an audience. The surah closes soon after with the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ told to say: I ask no payment for this, and I'm not one who pretends. Sincerity, at the start and at the end.

Choose one small thing you'll do today, a kindness, a task, a prayer if you pray, and look at the reason you're doing it. If part of it is for someone to notice, gently set that part down. Imagine doing it with no one ever knowing, only God, or only you, and see whether it feels lighter or harder.
Al-mukhlasin, those made sincere, the one group Iblis admits, in his own boast, that he can never mislead. Today's word.
Your line: the sincere are protected. Even Iblis, in his own boast, names that limit. Rest well.

558.title: Are they equal?
558.hook: are those who know and those who don't know equal (39:9)
558.carry: knowing isn't equal to not knowing
558.howItsDone: Muslims treat seeking knowledge as a religious duty; many attend study circles (halaqas) at mosques, and 39:9 is quoted to encourage study.

segments.voice: Yesterday: al-mukhlasin, the sincere, the limit Iblis named himself. Your line was the sincere are protected.

Some questions don't need an answer. Is a full glass heavier than an empty one? Would you rather be warm or freezing? A teacher asks one in class and nobody raises a hand, because the answer is sitting right there in the question. The Qur'an asks questions like this, and Surah Az-Zumar, the thirty-ninth, has one about knowing. You might expect it to start in a classroom. It starts in the middle of the night.
screen: `IT STARTS IN THE MIDDLE OF THE NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Verse nine opens with a picture. Someone is up in the hours of the night, prostrating and standing in prayer, wary of the hereafter, hoping for the mercy of their Lord. Is that person like the one who isn't? Then the famous line. Pickthall: "Are those who know equal with those who know not? But only men of understanding will pay heed." The answer is built in: no. But look at what knowing means here. It's not trivia. It sits right after the night prayer, the fear, the hope. Some commentators read the knowing in this verse as knowing your Lord and acting on it: the person who knows why they're awake in the night. So the verse sets learning and devotion side by side, and the tradition took that seriously. A hadith in Sahih Muslim says that whoever walks a path seeking knowledge, Allah makes easy for them a path to paradise. Another, in Ibn Majah, says seeking knowledge is an obligation on every Muslim, and scholars point out that this includes men and women alike. Then the last phrase: only people of understanding, ulu'l-albab, will take it to heart. Albab is the plural of lubb, a kernel, the inner core of a nut. People of understanding get to the core of things. Knowing and not knowing aren't the same, and the verse adds that it takes some knowing even to notice that.
screen: `A PATH TO KNOWLEDGE, A PATH TO PARADISE.`

segments.voice: If you have a book nearby, a Qur'an, a history, anything worth learning from, open it and read one page slowly, as if you'll be asked about it. If not, think of one subject you've always meant to understand better, and the first thing you'd read about it. Then sit with what you read, or chose, and let it settle to its kernel.
Lubb, a kernel, the inner core of a nut, the root of ulu'l-albab, those who get to the core of things. Today's word.
Your line: knowing isn't equal to not knowing. It starts with someone awake at night. Until tomorrow.

559.title: Don't despair
559.hook: O My servants who have wronged yourselves, don't despair of Allah's mercy, He forgives all sins (39:53)
559.howItsDone: Muslims seek forgiveness by saying astaghfirullah, often many times a day, and many scholars and preachers quote 39:53 to people who feel their sins are too great to be forgiven.

segments.voice: Yesterday: lubb, the kernel at the core of ulu'l-albab. Your line was knowing isn't equal to not knowing.

A group of men come to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. They've done terrible things: killed many times, and committed adultery many times. They've listened to his message, and they like it. But they say their problem straight. What you're calling us to is good. If only you could tell us there's a way to make up for what we've done. They aren't arguing. They're asking whether it's already too late. A report in Sahih al-Bukhari says the answer came as revelation, and one of the verses was this one.

Surah Az-Zumar, verse fifty-three. Pickthall: "Say: O My slaves who have been prodigal to their own hurt! Despair not of the mercy of Allah, Who forgiveth all sins. Lo! He is the Forgiving, the Merciful." Start with the address. Ya 'ibadiya, O My servants. Before a word about what they did, Allah calls them His. People who have gone too far against their own souls, and still addressed as Mine. The first command isn't do this or do that. It's: don't despair. La taqnatu. The verb names the despair of someone who has stopped expecting anything, and the verse forbids it before it promises anything else. Then the promise: He forgives all sins, jami'an, every one of them. Scholars read this with the very next verse: turn to your Lord and submit to Him before the punishment comes. The door is wide, and the way through it is turning back. Some early authorities are reported to have called it the most hopeful verse in the Qur'an. And notice who it was for: not people with small slips, but men who had killed. Teachers draw the point out. If the verse reached them, it reaches the person who skipped their prayers for a month, broke a promise, or fell back into an old habit. In that reading, the danger isn't only the mistake. It's deciding the mistake is the end.

Think of one good habit you let slip: a prayer, a walk, a call to a parent, this very path if you missed some days. When a voice says it's too late, or you always do this, hear the verse's first words instead: O My servants. Then choose the smallest way back, not to make up for everything, just to return; if you pray, you can say astaghfirullah.
Don't despair. Az-Zumar fifty-three: to people who have wronged themselves, never lose hope in Allah's mercy, for He forgives all sins to those who turn back. Today's word.
Your line: never despair of mercy. Even men who had killed were still called His servants. See you tomorrow.

560.howItsDone: Muslims greet one another with as-salamu 'alaykum, peace be upon you, the same greeting the Qur'an says the angels give at the garden's gates, and are encouraged to keep good company.

segments.voice: Yesterday: don't despair, the verse for people who had gone too far. Your line was never despair of mercy.

Watch the doors of a wedding hall, a stadium, a graduation. People rarely arrive alone. They come in clusters: a family, a carload of friends, a team in matching shirts. You can tell who belongs with whom by who they're walking beside. Surah thirty-nine is named for that. Zumar: groups, crowds, companies. At its very end, it pictures the Day of Judgment not as a long line of individuals, but as people arriving in groups, and the gates they arrive at.

Verse seventy-one: those who denied are driven toward hell in groups. When they arrive, its gates are opened, and its keepers ask: didn't messengers come to you? Verse seventy-three: those mindful of their Lord are led to the garden in groups. When they arrive, and its gates have been opened, its keepers say: salamun 'alaykum, peace be upon you. You've done well, so enter, to stay. Now a small detail in the Arabic. In the first verse, its gates are opened: futihat. In the second, there's an extra and: wa futihat, and its gates have been opened. Some commentators read that and as meaning the garden's gates were already open, waiting, like a host who unlocks the door before the guests reach the house. And the first words are peace. Not a test, not a question. A greeting. Elsewhere the Qur'an says each person comes to Him alone; here, at the gates, they arrive together. Then verse seventy-four: the people say, praise be to Allah, who has fulfilled His promise to us. The surah ends with the angels circling the Throne, and the words: praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds. Look back across this week and the same arc shows: peace on all the messengers; Dawud bowing when he saw his mistake; Ayyub's spring after long illness; the sincere that Iblis can't reach; the one who prays at night and knows; mercy for those who'd gone too far. And now groups of people walking together toward open gates, greeted with peace.
screen: `PRAISE TO THE LORD OF THE WORLDS.`

segments.voice: Picture the people you spend most of your time with as a group, walking somewhere together. Which way are they walking, and who leaves you steadier than they found you? Hold one of them in mind and, if you pray, thank God for them; if not, simply be grateful, and think of one person you'd like to walk beside more often.
Zumar: groups, crowds, companies, the name of the surah whose last verses picture the mindful led to the garden together. Today's word.
Your line: greeted with peace. A week of mercy ends at an open gate. Day five hundred sixty, and the week is done.

original.note: Arabic: in groups, in companies, the word that names surah thirty-nine.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Day is only about standing alone.
what it means: Az-Zumar pictures people led in groups, and the garden's gates open with a greeting of peace.

what a scholar hears: 19:95 has each one coming alone, while 39:71–73 has them arriving zumar; 39:71 has futihat, 39:73 wa futihat; some tafsir read the added waw as the gates already open, honoring the arrivals.
recall: the kernel, the core of the mind

chat.says: Why is Surah Az-Zumar called 'the groups'?
options: Its end pictures people arriving in groups, the mindful greeted with peace.
It's named for the crowds who gathered to hear the Prophet preach in Mecca.
It names the tribes of Arabia and lists which ones accepted Islam first.
chat.meaning: Zumar means groups: verses 71 to 73 picture people driven and led to the gates in groups, the mindful greeted with peace.
